column3: Efficiency is part of building any company. I get it.
column11:
Efficiency is part of building any company. I get it.

But the problem starts when GTM spend goes down… and revenue expectations go up.

Being disciplined about CAC makes sense. But reducing spend removes the crucial part of building, scaling GTM - all the reach, experimentation, and ultimately - staying visible on the market ✌️

all of which eventually influence the CAC, the efficiency….

Predictable pipeline usually sits on top of a lot of unglamorous work:

- Ongoing testing
- Consistent market presence
- Regular feedback from the team, customers, and prospects

When those inputs shrink because we cut down on costs on revneue team, the impact doesn’t always show up immediately. It shows up a quarter later (fewer deals, thinner pipelines, longer sales cycles, etc)

Revenue rarely grows when the effort behind it shrinks. Reducing costs can absolutely work

but only if the system itself is improved, not just scaled back

P.S. How do you balance cost discipline with maintaining momentum?

column3: Most B2B GTM runs channels in isolation. Demand gen, outbound, retention all in their own silos.
column11:
Most B2B GTM runs channels in isolation. Demand gen, outbound, retention all in their own silos.
Here are the 6 stages we connect into one loop, so each one makes the next cheaper.

Here's the breakdown:

→ Stage 1 · Generate demand
↳ Content, paid, outbound, partnerships
↳ Where does your buyer actually spend time? Start there.

→ Stage 2 · Identify who's paying attention
↳ Lead magnets, forms, social engagement, and organic followers
↳ If traffic doesn't turn into something you own, you can't capture it

→ Stage 3 · Stay in the room
↳ SDR sequences, newsletter, community, events, retargeting
↳ Most of the pipeline you need this quarter is already in your database
↳ They're just not ready yet, so nurture + (always) stay top of mind

→ Stage 4 · Earn the trust
↳ Sales-led: get the call booked
↳ Product-led: get them to first value (e.g Amplitude )
↳ Before either happens, they've already read your case studies, watched your demo, and used your free tool

→ Stage 5 · Score and route automatically
↳ Clay and HubSpot score every inbound signal against your ICP
↳ High fit goes to sales immediately
↳ Low fit goes back into nurture
↳ 90% of this doesn't need a human in the loop anymore

→ Stage 6 · Land and expand
↳ Retention is underrated as a growth channel
↳ Clients who stay become your case studies (e.g Swarm, Clustr)
↳ Case studies become your best top-of-funnel

Why the whole thing compounds:

↳ Cold outreach converts better when prospects already recognize the brand
↳ The content that performs organically tells you what to put a budget behind
↳ Your paid audiences and your outbound lists overlap more than most people realize
↳ Every engagement signal from every stage sharpens the next campaign

We use HubSpot and Clay for scoring and routing in stage 5. Common Room, Trigify, and Factors.ai  to pick up 1st-party engagement signals in stage 2.

Each one makes the next stage more efficient.

Not every path needs to be running. But every stage should have at least one.

column3: Teams that combine multiple signals close 3-4x more pipeline than teams running funding alerts. Here's the difference, and how to run ABM:
column11:
Teams that combine multiple signals close 3-4x more pipeline than teams running funding alerts. Here's the difference, and how to run ABM:

Triggers are public events.
→ Series A closed. New VP Sales hired. Installed competitor.

Signals are private behaviors from the buying committee.

→ 3 buyers from one account on /pricing this week. Champion engaged 3x with your LinkedIn this week. VP of Marketing downloaded the content.

The problem with triggers: they're public.
Every SDR with a Crunchbase login can pull the same Series B list Monday morning.

By Tuesday afternoon, 40 SDRs sent the same "congrats on the raise" email.

Your prospect ignores all of them.

→ Trigger window dies in 14 days. After that, you're another cold email.

→ Signal window dies in 24-48 hours. If you don't use it in time, they might book a demo with someone else.

Most teams never get past triggers.

Only 25% of B2B teams use real intent data.
The other 75% are still sending "congrats on the raise" emails.

Here's how we run ABM at Growth Today:

1 trigger = the reason to reach out.
3 signals = proof they're considering it right now. (or have a need + urgency)

One Tier 1 account, properly stacked:

→ New VP Sales hired (trigger)
→ 3 buyers from the company on /pricing this week (signal)
→ Champion engaged 3x with your LinkedIn this week (signal)
→ Marketing engaged through retargeting ads (signal)

Four reasons to send an email. Each is strong on its own.

Reply rates: 5-12% on a stacked signal account. 1-3% on a trigger-only account.

The difference: your messaging reads like you've been paying attention. Not like you ran a Crunchbase  export.

Here's where most ABM programs break:

Sales chases the 5 trigger accounts. Marketing has no idea that those are the priority.
The other 95 accounts on the Tier 1 list get nothing.

→ No content
→ No ads
→ No retargeting

When a buyer from one of those 95 finally gives you intent data, nobody sees it.

The fix:

Sales and Marketing run the same Tier 1 list together.

→ Marketing covers all 95 with content, ads, and retargeting. ZenABM , HubSpot
→ Sales puts higher effort on the trigger-stacked accounts. Clearbit Apify 6sense , CommonRoom etc.

That's signal-based ABM.
Not 5 news alerts on the same account in a CRM.

Most B2B teams run outbound like it’s only a bottom‑of‑funnel channel.

So reply rates are usually SUPER SMALL.

But if you think about it, outbound actually follows the exact same structure as content:

Attract → Nurture → Convert.

Because at the end, we’re talking to PEOPLE.
AND Prospects are like… dating 👀
Not everybody is ready or wants to be with you

YET 😉

So here’s how the best GTM teams run it.

Step 1: Attract (Top of funnel)

↳ Signals from your market
↳ Broad triggers that show relevance
↳ Low‑friction outreach

Examples:

→ hiring signals
→ funding announcements
→ new product launches
→ website visits
→ LinkedIn engagement

Tools teams use here: Clay , Common Room, RB2B, Apollo.io, LinkedIn Sales Navigator

Goal: Start conversations with accounts entering a buying window. Not hard sell.

Step 2: Nurture (Middle of funnel)

↳ Conversations already started
↳ Signals show real interest
↳ Now you build trust

Examples:

→ prospects replying “not now”
→ multiple stakeholders engaging
→ repeat website visits
→ demo page visits

Best teams move these accounts into:

→ content nurture
→ relevant insights
→ lightweight follow‑ups

Tools: HubSpot, n8n, Claude workflows, email sequencing tools

Goal: Stay top of mind until timing becomes right.

Step 3: Convert (Bottom of funnel)

↳ Accounts showing clear buying signals
↳ Multiple touches have already happened

Now outreach becomes:

→ case studies
→ proof
→ tailored outreach
→ direct meeting asks

Signals often include:

→ pricing page visits
→ multiple buyers engaging
→ direct replies

Goal: Move qualified accounts to meetings.

Most outbound fails because teams skip the first two stages.
They jump straight to “convert”.
But buyers rarely start there.

The best GTM teams run outbound like a funnel: Attract → Nurture → Convert.

Just like content.

Subject lines

↳ Remove: "AI", nuzzwords, numbers, and questions → -9%, -4%, -7% fewer open

Email length

↳ 1 sentence emails: 1.9% reply. 3 sentences: 2.9%. Write 3 sentences.
↳ Keep it under 100 words. It gets ~50% higher reply rate than anything longer

Personalization type

↳ Activity-based (what they actually did): 24% direct reply rate
↳ Company-level: 9%
↳ No personalization: 2%

Words that hurt your reply rates

↳ "AI" in the body: −36%
↳ "Platform" or "solution": −26%
↳ Buzzwords: −57%
↳ Write the way you talk on a call (not the way you write a landing page)

CTA

↳ Making an offer: +28%
↳ One CTA only. Don’t use multiple CTA-s.
↳ The top CTA globally in 2025 was a soft ask, not "book a 30-minute call"

Sequences

↳ 58% of all replies come from Email 1
↳ First bump adds +49%
↳ Email 5 drops −55% vs baseline
↳ 1-sentence bump = 2× more replies than a longer bump
↳ Breakup email: +89% vs a standard bump
↳ Stop at 4–6 emails. End with a breakup, not another pitch.

How to cold email like the top 1%

Step 1: Fix the car’s engine before you drive the car

Before anyone touches copy, we check the foundation.

↳ Is the targeting actually good, or just filtered by persona and company size?
↳ Is the data accurate and up to date? Do we have a system in place to keep it accurate?
↳ Are emails landing in the inbox at all? Do we have a deliverability system in place?

Don’t spend a week on copy when the segmentation strategy was wrong from day one.
It’s like fixing the colour of the car when the engine doesn’t run.

We use Clay  for all signals, enrichment, tiering, and scoring, all in one place.
We use EmailBison  and EmailGuard to run our automated email infrastructure.

Step 2: Test ONE thing at a time

New ICP. New angle. New tool. Never all three at once.

↳ Change one variable per test → targeting, copy, sequence structure
↳ If two things change at once, you learn nothing
↳ If you slow down to get the right foundation, you get to the desired outcome faster

Step 3: Build feedback loops

Start paying attention to:

↳ Which segments actually replied (vertical, persona, signal)
↳ Where people stopped responding (which step, on what angle, why)
↳ Which objections came up more than once

If you are building outbound from scratch right now, make learning the #1 KPI.
No meetings booked. Learning.

Step 4: Write down and systemize what works

When something starts performing, document it.
Then systemize it.

↳ Segmentation and targeting logic that worked
↳ Deliverability standards that outperform other patterns
↳ Messaging patterns that came from real conversations

Here is what healthy looks like for reference:

Connection acceptance rate: 30–40% = healthy · 50%+ = strong
Cold email reply rate: 3–8% = stable · 10%+ = strong
Positive reply rate: 8–12% = healthy
Bounce rate: under 3% = safe

If you are below these, the problem is usually in Step 1 or Step 3.
Not the copy.

Outbound gets less exciting once it is structured.
(This is how you know it’s working)

No go-to-market channel does not change that much.
The channel only amplifies what is already working underneath it.

column3: How to do ABM like the top 1%:
column11:
How to do ABM like the top 1%:

1. Buying-committee > Single-person

One person = curiosity. 1-3% response rate
Two+ = committee forming. 3-4x higher response rate

→ Build your triggers around account-level activity, not JUST person-level.

2. Trigger-based > Cadence-based

A: M/W/F on a fixed cadence
B: reaching out within 2-4 hours of a high-value signal: pricing page visit, repeat content engagement, job change.
(bare minimum to stay top of mind)

→ Build your sequencer around their intent and engagements. Nurture them if they're not ready. 

3. Multi-channel > Single-channel

Pick one channel and run 5-7 touches on it
vs. 3-7% response rate Email, LinkedIn, and call with 2-3 touches: 5-12% response rate

→ Stop one-channel approach (good MVP). Orchestrate across three.

4. Reply triage playbook > Ad-hoc

Old school: handle replies ad-hoc, no playbook.
New school: specific rule of engagement:

→ Positive → demo invite sent within 24h
→ "Not now" → 90-day nurture sequence triggered automatically
→ Wrong person → multi-thread the account + ask for a referral in the same reply

→ Have clear rules of engagement for your common scenarios + make the execution easy for SDRs.

We can help with that and triage these through HubSpot Salesforce  + Instantly, Smartlead/preferred sequencer.

5. Account-based ROI math > Per-email ROI math

One account, 5 messages, 1 reply, $200k deal
vs. 5,000 emails, 50 replies, 0 deals

→ Do ABM and combine ads + content + email. (eg. use ZenABM )

6. Regularly update your ICP > Quarterly, take a look at old dashboards

Have no ICP doc/messaging - update quarterly,
vs. auto-update your tiered accounts & contacts, source new ICP fit companies, and tier them out.

Clear ICP + strong data foundation + iterative messaging matrix = lower CAC

column3: R.I.P. cold email copy as the way to fix reply rate.
column11:
R.I.P. cold email copy as the way to fix reply rate.
16% of B2B emails go to spam in 2026 (Validity). 90% inbox placement gets 5.3% reply rate. Below 70% gets 0.8%. (Smartlead). Here is what to do:

1. SPF, DKIM, DMARC

If you don’t set this up, your inbox will get a HUGE spam rate within 2-3 weeks of sending.

↳ Run a check with MX Toolbox, GSuite, Instantly, Smartlead’s checker before the next campaign.

2. Use the secondary domain, never the primary.

Sending cold from your primary domain is how you can get your domain burnt, negatively impacting your day-to-day business.

↳ Buy secondary domains, never use your primary domain for cold emails

3. 2 inboxes per secondary domain

Gmail and Outlook flag domains with too many senders. Cap at 2 per domain. Not 1 domain with 12 mailboxes.

↳ 2 inboxes at 5 domains gets you 10 inboxes to start.

4. Warmup 2-4 weeks before the first cold send

Brand new domain sending 50 cold emails on day one is a death sentence. Warm up 4-8 weeks before launch using Instantly, Smartlead. No short cuts.

↳ 2- 4 weeks of warmup w/o cold emailing.

5. Bounce rate <2%

Verify 100% of your list with MillionVerifier , MailNinja, lemlist and ZeroBounce before any send. If the list is older than 30 days, re-verify it.

↳ Re-validate any lists older than 30 days. Always.

6. 5-20 cold emails per inbox per day.

Spikes look like spam. 200 emails Monday and 20 Tuesday flags you faster than a steady 20 a day. Both Instantly and Smartlead auto-throttle for a reason. Use it.

↳ Consistent low sending > spikes burning your inboxes

7. Plain text only. No HTML, no images, no tracking pixels.

HTML emails read as marketing emails to Gmail's filters.

↳ If you wouldn't type it as a Slack DM to a coworker, don't send it cold.

8. Monitor Inbox placements weekly

Don't assume you're landing in the inbox. Test with GlockApps, MailReach, or Instantly, Smartlead's built-in tool weekly. Inbox vs spam vs promotions.

↳ Stop guessing. Test the actual placement.

9. Engagement signal management

Keep your warm-up active while you’re cold emailing. Send more warm-up than cold emails.

↳ Replies improve placement. Bounces and unsubs reduce it.

10. Move DMARC from p=none to p=reject within 90 days

Most teams set DMARC to `p=none` (monitoring only) and never enforce. Inbox providers flag domains stuck on `none` because spoofers love them

↳ Move to `p=quarantine` after 30 days, `p=reject` after 90.

Don’t open a doc and start editing copy when the reply rate decreases.
The other way around.

If your email is in spam, the copy, your offer, simply doesn’t matter.

Before you write a word, look up what is happening at their company right now. Hiring, funding, and a new product. Use the real thing. Not "Hi {First Name}" with the name swapped in.

Medium fit: mix of manual + automated steps, fewer touchpoints

↳ Copilots draft replies, call summaries, and research briefs. A human reviews.
↳ One shared prompt library. One owner accountable.
↳ Track hours saved and quality, not "we use AI".

→ Stage 3 · Augmented / Workflow automation (12 rules)
↳ Enrichment waterfall plus AI scoring on fit and intent.
↳ Signal-triggered sequences, not static lists.
↳ A human review gate before every send.

What kills you here: automating outreach on inaccurate / not relevant target accounts, building ANYTHING on top of bad data. 

→ Stage 4 · Orchestrated / Supervised agents (15 rules)
↳ Agents research and draft. Humans approve.
↳ Escalation design: define what agents can and cannot do alone.
↳ One operator supervises many agents (lowest cost per opportunity).

↳ Agent-orchestrated across sales, marketing, and CS.
↳ Governance-in-the-loop: humans' own strategy and exceptions.
↳ Data platform built for production AI, not bolted on.

What kills you here: scaling autonomy faster than governance.

The mistake almost everyone makes: running tomorrow's needs on yesterday's processes. You can't figure out all the pieces, and done is better than perfect, but make sure you don't build highly impactful areas on broken GTM motion or untested and undocumented processes.

Cold email vs LinkedIn DMs vs cold calling vs paid ads. Pick the channel based on the account value, not the other way around. Here is the rule we use across scaling B2B SaaS:

What each channel does:

↳ Cold email = volume engine. 500 to 2,000 sends a day. Direct pitch is fine.
↳ LinkedIn DMs = precision play. 40 DMs a day, capped. Value first, no hard ask.
↳ Cold calling = breakthrough channel. 50 to 100 dials a day. Real-time, adaptive.
↳ Paid ads = warming layer. Familiarity before any outreach lands.

The rule we follow:

↳ Tier 1 accounts get all 4 channels orchestrated together. Paid ads warm. LinkedIn nurtures. Cold call breaks through. Cold email only if the offer fits.
↳ Tier 2: get cold email at scale, plus paid ads as the warming layer.
↳ Tier 3: No LinkedIn DM. No cold call, just emails at scale.

What breaks the rule:

↳  Push Tier 1 into a cold email campaign, and you burn the relationship
↳  Scale LinkedIn past 40 DMs a day, and your LinkedIn stops working (you can’t reach all leads if LinkedIn connection requests are capped at 100 / week)
↳  Run cold calls with no warming layer, and connect rates are lower
↳  Run paid ads with no outbound

Email: Instantly, Smartlead, EmailBison  + EmailGuard, MailReach  (deliverability)
Ads: ZenABM , Fibbler, Satlo, FactorsAI (mid-market), 6sense, Demandbase  (enterprise)

signal-based hooks. the 3W frameworks. "best practice" sequences.

Fear of standing out.
Fear of sounding different.
Fear of being rejected as yourself.

Cold email copy doesn’t need more tricks.

It needs more honesty. and YOU.

1️⃣ I write to my favorite prospect: I picture one person who could be my ideal client, writing email copy in the same words and tone of voice as I'd talk to them.

2️⃣ I say what I actually believe about what we can and can't do: we're not good for everybody. We also cannot help everybody, & I try to be super transparent about what is realistic or not.

3️⃣ I use AI to amplify my thinking: what to say, how to reach out, when to follow up (although, thanks to HubSpot, lemlist, and our fancy Make automations, I couldn't realistically forget anyway…)

Signal-based outreach has a 35-40% reply rate when done right. Here are the four dimensions that decide whether signals actually work:

Dimension 1: Signal type

Not all signals are the same. Rank them instead by purchase correlation:

↳ #1 Former customers at a new company → trust already built, fastest proof of value
↳ #2 New leadership ≤90 days → they are still deciding what to change. Day 60 is when they are most open to new vendors.
↳ #3 Website behavior → pricing page = 80pts, demo page = 100pts, 25-30% reply rate because they already know you
↳ #4 Tech stack change → removed a competitor from their stack = active buying window right now
↳ #5 Expansion → new funding, new region, new product = They are growing faster than their current setup can handle
↳ #6 Hiring or downsizing → both signal budget and priority areas

Don’t filter by company size and industry. Those are the weakest signals on this list.

Tools: Warmly, · BuiltWith · Trigify.io · Clay · Bombora

Dimension 2: Signal freshness

↳ Last 24 hours: 1.5x multiplier → act now
↳ Last 7 days: 1.2x → still strong
↳ Last 14 days: 1.0x → baseline
↳ 30+ days ago: 0.3x → almost worthless

50% of the signal value is lost after 7 days.
Don’t batch your outreach weekly.
You do not want to run on signals that have already expired.

Tools: Clay timestamp columns · Slack real-time alerts · N8N routing.

Don’t run outreach on outdated data.
Data foundation is a MUST.

Dimension 3: Signal combination

One signal on the right list = 8-10% reply rate.
Three signals stacked = 35-40%.

↳ Pricing page visit (80pts) + Champion job change (75pts) + Bombora (40pts) = 195pts → reach out within 1 hour
↳ Funding (45pts) + Hiring (40pts) + 3 blog visits (20pts) = 105pts → personalized sequence within 24 hours
↳ Website visit (10pts) + LinkedIn engagement (30pts) = 40pts → nurture first, not direct ask

The score tells you the motion.
Not the message. The motion. When and what’s the right ask

These are the tools you can use: Clay scoring formula · Common Room · HubSpot lead scoring · Koala

Don't treat everyone equally. A pricing page visit is not the same as a blog read.

Dimension 4: Response speed

5-minute response = 21x more likely to convert.

↳ VP on your pricing page: respond within 1 hour
↳ Champion job change detected: wait until day 30, then reach out. Reference the work you did together at their old company.
↳ Competitor removed from their stack: a few days or weeks before they find someone else

The signal is the alarm.
The SLA is what you do when it goes off.

Tools: Slack · n8n · Clay · HubSpot

column11:
My hands used to shake before cold calls. Now I actually look forward to them 🙌 

Not because I suddenly became good at sales but because I stopped guessing

Confidence doesn't come from being naturally smooth or extroverted.

It comes from preparation.

When you know exactly what to say, when to say it, and why it matters, the nerves disappear.

So I mapped out the 4 parts every cold call needs:

01. Focus → Who are we calling?

- ICP
- Key roles
- ROI narrative

02. Positioning → Who would they care?

- Talk track
- Competitive angle
- Insight line

03. Pitch → What do we say to earn a conversation?

- 10 second opener
- Soft assumption
- Discovery question

04. Outreach → How do we reach them?

- Relevance hook
- Warm context
- Call timing

This isn't about being perfect.

Now I can walk into every call knowing the next possibility.

And that changes everything.

column3: Most outbound CTAs ask for something before giving anything. ”Do you have time for a quick chat?" → everybody sends this.
column11:
Most outbound CTAs ask for something before giving anything. ”Do you have time for a quick chat?" → everybody sends this.

In a commoditized market, it's exactly why nobody responds.

When a buyer can't tell you apart from the 50 other agencies or tools pitching them the same outcome, a meeting request gives them no reason to say yes.

A meeting is work 💼 for them. 

Your CTA has to earn it.

Here's a simple way to make these better: 

Instead of "let me pitch you." 
Use this: "Here's something I already put together for you."

It proves you understand their world before asking them to trust that you do.

We mapped 20 templates across 4 categories from paid media, creative, CRO, full-funnel, outbound, and SaaS.

The structure that works every time:
"I [did a specific thing related to their business]. Can I send it over?"

The more specific the observation, the higher the response rate.

The generic value doesn't land. tailored observation does. 

Save this. 
Try one this week.

What CTA format is working best for you right now?

column11:
I have 3x'd my impressions in the last 3 weeks.
Here is the exact system behind it.

1. Start with one problem and one person

↳ Name one problem you have already solved and can prove with a number
↳ Name one person who has that problem and has the budget to fix it
↳ Test it: write one sentence. "I help [person] [result] in [timeframe]."
↳ If that sentence takes more than 10 words, it is still too broad

2. Write for what they already believe and struggle with, not what you want them to think

↳ What are they trying to avoid right now?
↳ What would they screenshot and send to someone else?
↳ Do they buy based on one post or after watching you for 3 months?
↳ For most B2B GTM teams: they need to see the system working before they pay for it

3. Your profile either converts or it does not

↳ Headline: who you help, what you get them, one proof point
↳ Featured section: one resource that solves one specific problem
↳ About: written for them, not about you
↳ If someone cannot tell what you do in 3 seconds, they move on

4. Post with the right content ratio, not just consider the posting frequency

ToF 1 to 2x per week:
↳ Data reveals trends that attract people who do not know you yet
↳ Contrarian angles you can actually back up

MoF 3 to 4x per week:
↳ Show the system, not just the outcome
↳ Break down principles, frameworks, and decisions step by step
↳ Address the real reasons people hesitate to buy

BoF once a week:
↳ Real results with before and after numbers
↳ Genuinely useful content drops

5. Name the result, not the service

Vague: "We run LinkedIn content."
Specific: "3 posts a week. Within 90 days, most clients get 1 to 3 inbound meetings a month without running ads."

The more specific the result, the faster someone you can persuade to take action.

6. Build your offer into your profile before you ask anyone to buy

Featured section:
↳ First slot: a free resource that solves one specific problem today
↳ Second slot: your newsletter or a short course → they join, they see how
you think, they start trusting the work
↳ Third slot: your main offer with a booking link

The booking link matters more than most people think.
If someone reads 10 posts and wants to talk, they should be able to book in 15 seconds.
If they have to DM you and wait, half of them drop off.

Earn the right to sell before you sell.
Post for 60 days. Give value first. Make the offer easy to find.
When someone is ready, the profile does the rest.

6 things we keep seeing go wrong across 157+ B2B clients.(… what we do instead 👇)

1️⃣ Reply rates drop → send more emails

More emails to the wrong people don't work. 
We score every contact before it goes into a sequence. 
500 people who fit → more replies than 5,000 who don't.

→ Clay agents and HubSpot auto-filters by ICP fit and signal before anything goes to a sequence

2️⃣ Nothing works → rewrite the copy

Check where emails actually land before touching a word. 
Native Gmail and Outlook infra outperforms SMTP relay on every campaign we've run.

→ Smartlead and Instantly.ai EmailBison help you with warming and running inbox placement tests

3️⃣ Everyone on the list gets a demo request

Some people have never heard of you. 
Asking them for a meeting is like proposing on a first date.

High Tier + Engaged contacts → ask for the meeting. Lower Tier or No Engagement → send something useful first. Then ask.

4️⃣ Outbound and marketing run separately

The people who book fastest have almost always seen your content before your email is sent. 
Run ads to the same accounts you're emailing. Give them content through organic LinkedIn, website, or through webinars. 
Same account list. Same timing. Coordinated motion. 

→ CommonRoom, Trigify.io, Factors.ai tracks who's engaging so outbound knows who to prioritize

5️⃣ One ICP definition for every channel

Funded SMB companies need a different angle than mid-market ones. 
3-6 weeks average sales close cycle is also different than 2-6 months.

Differentiate your outreach strategy by sales cycle, signal, and engagement history. 
Not just title and headcount.

6️⃣ Pipeline is slow → hire more people

More people doing the same thing that isn't working just costs more. 
Figure out what's broken first. 

Fix it. 
Then hire.

I ran my first outbound campaign 6 years ago. Drove 75 demos/mo for 2 E-Commerce SaaS as their growth leader, and then my cold email agency from 0 to $2M+ ARR. Here are 7 things I wish I knew before starting:

(1) Truly nail down your lead list

Sending your outreach messages to the right person matters more than anything else:

→ Precisely figure out what problem you're solving.
→ Find companies struggling with this problem.
→ Identify relevant individuals in these orgs.

(2) Give as much value as you can

You’re stepping into someone’s inbox uninvited.
& the fastest way to earn attention is to be USEFUL.

Give give give > ask

A simple approach:

→ Identify their problem
→ Share one practical solution for free
→ Do this as many times as you can on all channels where you are.

(Think through: why are you reading this LinkedIn post, right? EXACTLY!)

(3) Pick only one prospect and write for him/her

Many people try to write for 500k+ people.
Start with one instead.

Pick one prospect you’d genuinely want to work with.
& write as if they’re the only person receiving that email.

Then do the opposite:

→ Find 20 similar personas
→ Find similarities in their challenges, org size/org challenges
→ Then automate all these at a bigger scale

(4) Take care of the deliverability

Good deliverability doesn't guarantee your campaigns will succeed. But...

Bad deliverability guarantees your campaigns will fail.

Make sure to...

→ Send a few emails per mailbox (< 20 per day)
→ Set up MX, DMARK, SPF, DKIM records.
→ Disable open tracking.
→ Warm up mailboxes (bare minimum 14 days)
→ Weekly run inbox placement tests
→ Daily run domain blacklists checks

(5) Take the extra mile!! 

Any GTM channel is somewhat hard to crack. The same goes for cold email.

Make sure to go above and beyond when reaching out to your prospects:

→ Look at triggers, signals, current events, org. charts.

→ Reference insights from the job descriptions.

→ Don't stop at 1-2 email variations. At Growth Today, we frontload 8 variations

(6) Complement cold email with other GTM channels

Cold email is my favorite channel because it's cheaper to get started, and you can find what works a lot faster than with any other channel.

But it works even better with other channels.

→ Run ads to the same people you're cold emailing. warm them up! ♨️

→ Make great, authentic, and genuinely useful content and use email and LinkedIn to distribute it

→ Use cold emails to distribute valuable lead magnets.

(7) Don’t just use technology, leverage it to SYSTEMIZE

→ Have a look at growthtoday.co/sales-tools (or my fav one: our blog posts that include copy-pastable email templates)

→ Do a few tests manually to see what is the most interesting angle on the market to pitch your prospects.

→ Before hiring more people, ask: “Could I achieve the same with technology?”

→ Before doing more, ask: “Could I build a repeatable, scalable SOP or system instead of me doing this again and again?”

We analyzed 50B+ B2B email sends (Smartlead), 12M+ cold emails (Backlinko), and the public GTM motion of Gorgias, Rippling, Verkada, and Shopify.
Here is the order:

Most B2B teams build their GTM motion in the wrong order.

Activation is more exciting: clear ROI, fast wins, visible reps. Foundation work feels invisible.

But if you start there, the system stalls before it ever compounds.
You do not rise to the level of your goals. You fall to the level of your systems.

So here is how we audit every new client's pipeline before we touch any of their channels:

1. Build out the foundation

↳ Say your ICP pain out loud: repeat their pain in their own words
↳ Clarify your offer: Scaling a weak offer produces a lot of noise and no recurring revenue
↳ Name your enemy: give buyers something to remember you against
↳ Stack signals: funding round + GTM hire + engaged your content = one outreach trigger
↳ Protect the inbox: SPF, DKIM, DMARC, domain warm-up, copy never gets read from spam

Tools we usually connect here:

Clay, Apify, Trigify.io, Common Room // Communication Design 

2. Strategize

↳ Let triggers write the copy: company hires a GTM engineer? That IS the email
↳ Run multiple channels: Content builds awareness. Outbound activates intent. Ads reinforce both.
↳ Narrow down your ICP: “B2B SaaS” is a category vs. ”Series A SaaS with an existing inbound team” is a real target.
3. Execute

↳ Content: Builds the audience before outreach ever starts.
↳ Signal‑based outbound: Reach out when something actually happened.
↳ Retargeting Ads should follow engagement, not random targeting.

Tools here usually look like:

lemlist, EmailBison, expandi.net, LinkedIn Ads

We systemize these to make sure they compound.

4. Amplify

↳ Boost posts that already booked meetings, don't guess what to pay to promote
↳ Repurpose your best-performing content into content-led outbound sequences
↳ Run lookalike campaigns against your closed-won accounts

Stack we use:
Dock, HubSpot, Fellow AI 

5. Scale

↳ Systematize what worked: document the triggers, the copy, the list criteria
↳ Add channels only after layers 1 and 2 are solid
↳ Replace manual steps with agents once the process proves out

Pipeline compounds when the foundation is right.

Most teams are building from layer 3 up (activation). That’s why it doesn’t work:

You can’t build the roof on the house if the floors are missing:

Foundation = data.
Architecture = signals + enrichment.
Activation = manual (SDRs, AEs) + AI SDRs.
GTM Co-pilot = the final layer, once the system runs itself.

column3: SDRs and GTM Engineers and AEs are not the same.
column11:
SDRs and GTM Engineers and AEs are not the same.

I still see teams hire SDRs and expect them to build the system too.

They ask them to fix Clay tables, clean HubSpot, route signals, and maintain n8n workflows.

Then they hire a GTM Engineer and ask why meetings are not getting booked.

Both roles matter.
They just own different parts of a modern AI-native outbound motion.

We build this split for clients all the time, and the handoff needs to be clear.

Step 1 → SDR is responsible for generating the meeting and the feedback loop
↳ Work Tier 1 accounts first and closely with the AE-s
↳ call, email, LinkedIn, and follow-up
↳ test angles and objections in real conversations (feed this back to the GTM Engineer)
↳ turn signal context into booked meetings (GTM Engineer creates this for him/her)

Example:
↳ If an account engaged with content, visited pricing, and has a new VP, the SDR uses that context to cold call the lead + reach out

Step 2 → GTM Engineers own system design and messaging that works for the SDRs and carry quota for automated outbound
↳ build ICP logic, scoring, and tiering
↳ connect Clay , HubSpot, Claude , Common Room, N8N, other tools
↳ set enrichment waterfalls and data rules, and govern the data with Ops
↳ route intent signals into the right sequence or rep queue
↳ audit what works and improve conversion paths and the full funnel

Example:
↳ When 500 lookalike accounts are sourced through Clay, the GTM Engineer scores fit + signal, pushes Tier 1 into the SDR queue, and sends Tier 2 into nurture, Tier 3 for automated outreach. 

Contact and company fields created and updated in HS and SFDC, build new marketing/sales-related custom fields + dashboards

Step 3 → Both roles work better with a clean boundary
↳ SDRs should spend time selling and testing new angles before automating these (or work closely with GTM engineers through growth sprints)
↳ GTM Engineers should build the engine and carry pipeline goals for programmatic motion, but act as true owners and enablers for SDRs to properly prospect high-value accounts.

You can experiment a lot more effectivel + make the pipeline generation more predictable and repeatable when these experts work together and not against each other, so amplify each other's strengths.

column3: what we changed to fix their outbound
column11:
what we changed to fix their outbound

One thing I love about outbound is how quickly the truth shows itself.

If the system is off, the results will drag. If the system is right, everything clicks.... even if nothing else changes.

Last week we worked with a services company whose outbound “felt flat.”

But once we dug in, the problem wasn’t just list or the copy
…it was that their system was fighting against them.

Here’s exactly what we changed:

1️⃣ We stopped selling the service at scale only a few people respond to

They have 3 services.

All great.
But one is a terrible conversation starter.

Cold prospects don’t wake up thinking:

“Wow I really hope someone offers me a 40-page report today.”

Their prospects literally respond ~2× better to the other 2 services, but outbound wasn’t aligned to that.

So we repositioned around their two strongest conversation starters

2️⃣ We fixed the invisible killer → deliverability

Their audience = mid-market + enterprise.

Enterprise = Microsoft.

Microsoft = “I will evaluate your entire family tree before letting your email through.” 😅

So yep… we’re have a different mix Google + Microsoft inboxes and all these inboxes are purchased to multiple resellers, so we can continously monitor which ones are performing the best and use the data from our inbox placement tests to make adjustments to keep hitting the inbox.

3️⃣ We replaced the “quick chat?” CTA with value

Their CTA used to be a meeting request. (in a soft way which is GOOD).

But (especially in the agency space), you’re likely selling something that is “easy” to execute, so the barrier to entry is low.

So we introduced CTAs that give something instead of ask for something:

- campaign ideas
- roundtable theme maps
- insight drops
- quick audits

Concrete example if you’re running an ad agency:

→ “I have analyzed your ads published in the last 90 days. Can I send over a quick audit to decrease the CPL?”

→ “Would you be open to exploring how we can help you decrease the CPL on your Meta ads?”

GIVE → GIVE → GIVE → before you ASK.

4️⃣ We added intent + timing signals instead of guessing

Before: outbound went out in usual prospecting campaigns
Now: outreach triggers when something meaningful happens.

Signals we added:

→ new senior hires
→ hiring for marketing roles
→ aggressive ad spends
→ thought leadership indicators
→ content activity

5️⃣ We refreshed the messaging (just enough)

Not a rewrite — a refresh.

We updated angles based on:

the market’s current priorities
2026 plans
current challenges in their space
This avoids message fatigue

The fun part?

We didn’t change:

❌ the ICP
❌ the TAM
❌ the channel
❌ the core offer
❌ the send volume

Takeaway:

When outbound stops performing, people jump to copy first.

But the real leverage is almost always in:

→ targeting
→ timing
→ positioning
→ offer
→ infrastructure

Once the system is right, the copy suddenly becomes “amazing.”
Even if it’s the same copy you thought was the problem. 😅

An internet friend of mine, Eduard shared something that stuck with me:

Across all deals, no matter how good your product/service is, 20–35% close won is average.

And honestly… it makes sense.

Most prospects don’t say “no” because you’re bad.

They say “no” because right now isn’t the priority.

You can’t force timing.

Marketing helps you get seen, warm people up, educate them, and stay top-of-mind…

But it still can’t control when a company suddenly decides: “Okay, this just became urgent.”

And this is the part most teams forget:

If you can’t control when someone is ready,

then the only logical move is to make sure you’re always present when the moment happens.

Always. 💕

Which is exactly why signal-based, always-on outbound is such an easy win. 🏆

Most teams still run prospecting like this:
Build → send → finish → rebuild → repeat.

We’ve all done it.

But that approach makes it almost guaranteed you’ll miss people at the right time.

Because readiness rarely lines up with when you decide to run a campaign.

It usually shows up when something shifts on their side:

• budget changes • new leadership • pressure to hit numbers • new goals • new problems

Here’s what that means in practice 👇

1️⃣ Signals can tell you WHO is ready, not just who “fits the ICP”

Two companies can look identical on paper.

But only one is:

hiring for Demand Gen
posting thought leadership
running new ads
adding new leaders
changing their GTM team
promoting new initiatives

One is active.
The other is static.

2️⃣ You stop “guessing” and start “reacting”

When a new VP joins…
When a Head of Events gets hired…
When a team scales ad spend…
When leadership suddenly becomes very active online…

That’s your window.

Right. Then.

3️⃣ Your messaging becomes naturally relevant

You don’t need hyper-personalization but context.

Examples we used:

“Saw you’re hiring for Event Marketing — usually means the team is thinking a lot about pipeline. Could I share a few ideas?”

“Congrats on the new senior hire — would a few simple recommendations around X be helpful?”

“Noticed your ad spend is climbing — if mainstream channels aren’t giving you what you need, I can send a quick idea that’s been working well for similar teams.”

4️⃣ You stop exhausting the TAM

Usual prospecting motion = you work the static list you already have.

Signal-based outbound = you run always-on campaigns and surface new leaders, new accounts, and new activity as it happens.

It’s easier on the TAM and better for long-term performance.

5️⃣ Conversion rates lift without changing the copy

This is the part people underestimate.

Same message. Same CTA. Same structure.

But when it hits at the right time, the response rate looks completely different.

TAKEAWAY 🤩

Outbound is hard, and not getting easier

…and there are SO many gimmicks and so many tactics

but you cannot disagree that it’s a good idea to reach out to a prospect when there’s a real moment to do so ✌️

How we found winning angles for a $7M eCommerce SaaS expanding into Shopify SMBs

A client came to us wanting to grow in the Shopify / SMB segment.

They were doing well with enterprise and larger retail brands, but wanted to break into a new market with faster sales cycles.

Here’s what we found & how you can replicate the learnings for your motion 👇

1️⃣ Competitor-focused work better than reaching out to “out of market” accounts

When we reached out to competitor users directly , replies went up: 1 positive response for every 200 contacts.

Other angles performed decently (1 per 500–800 contacts), but competitor-led outreach clearly opened more conversations.

If your brand isn’t widely known yet, double down on:

- Building awareness (through ads, content, or community)
- Focusing on in-market companies already exploring your type of solution.

2️⃣ Re-prospecting TAM works

Most teams blast a list once and move on..But we went back to the same audience later:

→ new angles 
→ different offers 
→ different timing

Companies priorities change. Hitting the right person at the right time often happens on the second or third touch

If you don’t have a proven outbound motion yet, keep experimenting.

Once you find what works, layer in ads, PLG content, and community to reinforce awareness before outreach.

3️⃣ The sales cycle defines your outreach strategy

You’d think enterprise deals would be easier to prospect since the client already knew how to sell there.

Turns out, SMB brands replied faster and moved quicker through the funnel.

Shorter sales cycles = faster wins.

Here’s how you can use this insight to replicate it for your GTM motion:

Tier 1: 1:1 outreach by reps with calls, email + LinkedIn touches, longer delays between the steps 

Tier 2: 1:1 or hybrid/1:to many 

Tier 3: 1:many outreach by automation tools like Instantly.ai, Smartlead, EmailBison with fewer steps

4️⃣ Systemize early

Instead of constantly launching new campaigns, we built a repeatable motion around:

→ Evergreen competitor campaigns than run 24/7 by using Store Leads, BuiltWith 
→ Vertical message tests powered by signal-based targeting 
→ Tailored offers for in-market vs. out-of-market companies

What you can learn from this:

Neither using chatGPT/Claude threads for prospecting Nor Apollo import/export

A GTM system is built on top of these:

1️⃣ Layer 1: Data foundation

Clearly mapped out TAM with tiering/scoring, so you know where to prioritize your efforts and how

2️⃣ Layer 2: Activating data

Using triggers, insights into what the companies and contacts do. Like:

Capturing intent like visiting the website, engaging with your content on LinkedIn multiple times etc.

Scoring the contacts and companies to differentiate the outreach, motion, and offering.

3️⃣ Layer 3: GTM Co-pilot

Leveraging signals and intent, all connected, synced, and regularly updated in your CMR to run a highly autonomous or hybrid agent for prospecting or targeted ABM motion.

Before we automate anything at Growth Today, we run one test. We call it the Manual 30.

(like Forbes U30 but Manual U30 ✌️)

Open a simple sheet. Add 30 accounts you genuinely want to work with. Not random prospects. Not scraped lists. Companies you’d be proud to call clients.

Then go deep.

Layer 1: Buyer signals. Promotions. New mandates. Ad infos, 10-K report, and their initiatives. What they’re consistently talking about. What’s top of mind for them?

Layer 2: Company signals. Hiring insights. Expanding into new markets. Fresh funding. Sales leadership changes.

Layer 3: Thought leadership context Search their name + “podcast.” Search their name + “interview.”

Long-form conversations reveal operational tension people never post about.

Layer 4: Their GTM stack. CRM. Routing. Scheduling flow. Form logic.

Just by looking at their tech stack, you’ll know so much about how they operate and what GTM context their potential challenges are.

Layer 5: Process gaps. Job descriptions. Reviews. Case studies. Tells you what they’re focused on and what they’d like to actively solve

Layer 6: Job posts. Look at the language they use:

If this doesn’t generate real conversations, doing this at scale (by leveraging automation) will just help you fail faster.

& ONE MORE thing most teams underestimate: Speed-to-lead.

The longer they need to wait for your response, the lower your chances of turning that lead into a real conversation — and a booked meeting.

Strike while the iron is hot 🔥

column3: I used to think a “bad outbound month” meant we needed better copy.
column11:
I used to think a “bad outbound month” meant we needed better copy.

But this week reminded me (again) that copy is usually the least of the problems.

One of our clients in the services space came in thinking the same thing:

“Our messaging just isn’t strong enough.”

Except… that wasn’t purely the issue at all:

1️⃣ significant part of their target market is the enterprise

Enterprise prospects = Microsoft.

And Microsoft is picky.

If your infrastructure isn’t tuned for it, you can write the best email in the world, and nobody will see it.

I know many agencies in our space don’t do Microsoft (we do), but it’s SO true that Microsoft is just 5× harder.

So yep… we’re have a different mix of Google + Microsoft inboxes and all these inboxes are purchased by multiple resellers, so we can continuously monitor which ones are performing the best and use the data from our inbox placement tests to make adjustments to keep hitting the inbox.

2️⃣ they were leading with the wrong service

They have 3 services.

All great.

But one is a terrible conversation starter.

Their prospects literally respond ~2× better to the other 2 services, but outbound wasn’t aligned to that.

A tiny repositioning → big impact.

3️⃣ the CTA lacked compelling reasons to meet

In the agency space, you’re likely selling something that is “easy” to execute, so the barrier to entry is low.

What prospects see: “Everyone claims they do outbound, so I assume you’re all the same.”

This is commoditization.

The market is flooded and undifferentiated.

Because of this, you must be SO clear on how you’re different and give them a compelling reason to meet with you.

Concrete example if you’re running an ad agency:

→ “I have analyzed your ads published in the last 90 days. Can I send over a quick audit to decrease the CPL?”

→ “Would you be open to exploring how we can help you decrease the CPL on your Meta ads?”

#1 gives them something valuable for free.

GIVE → GIVE → GIVE → before you ASK.

4️⃣ They weren’t using any intent signals

General prospecting campaigns are good.

But if you’re only doing that, you don’t have any “always-on” campaigns that work 24/7 and indicate a buying window.

So we layered in:

→ new hires
→ accounts scaling ads
→ recent leadership hires
→ thought leaders actively posting/speaking at conferences

You can use Clay, Apollo (and many more) to test and capture these windows.

Same TAM.
Same volume.
Same (good) copy.

I’m confident there’ll be a completely different performance.

Because outbound doesn’t always have just a messaging problem.

It usually has a thought process problem.

Lesson I’m taking forward:

If outbound feels slow, don’t rush to rewrite the emails.

Check the infrastructure.
Check the timing.
Check the offer.
Check the CTA.
Check what buyers actually respond to in the first place.

Fix the system → the copy suddenly “works.”

Funny how that happens. 😅

column3: SaaS companies don’t buy the way we think they do.

SaaS decisions usually involve more than one person.

Those decisions usually live across teams.

Different people, different priorities.

Founders look at the big picture. Sales looks at the pipeline. RevOps cares about process. 

Tech worries about scalability, products, the roadmap, yada yada.

Everyone’s looking at the same challenge. Just from a different angle. 👀 

This is where a lot of GTM motions stop making sense.

When everything is aimed at one person, and we wait for a yes, we’re oversimplifying how SaaS actually buys.

What changed for me was thinking through:

Who else is involved? Who else influences the decision? Who else also needs to feel confident before anything moves?

lean thinking + rigorous process + fast execution.

proactive > vs. reactive

column3: Ok I know many of you would relate to this 😆, but…

Ok I know many of you would relate to this 😆, but…

Inside our clients’ playbooks, “send more emails” is step 10. The first 9 are system checks.

- founder says “let’s double outbound next quarter”
- team agrees
- sequences get expanded
- more leads get pulled
- volume goes up

Pipeline does not.

I do not say this to scare you. I say it because the fix is simple.

You do not need to stop outbound. You need to tune the engine first.

Here is how I walk leaders through it now.

Step 1 to 9 are not “nice to have.” They are your must have-s.

I ask them simple questions:

1- Do new leads go to the right owner by rule, not by hand?
2- Does each stage in your CRM have one clear owner?
3-Do you clean data on a clear plan, not “when we have time”?
4- Can one duplicate break your reports or forecasts?
5- Can a new lead sit forgotten for 3 days?

If we still smile after these, I add more.

1- Do teams hand off leads in one clear way each time?
2- Is “next step” clear in the CRM for each open deal?
3- Do gaps in activity ping someone on your team?
4- Does someone check pipeline hygiene each week?

When we see “no” in many places, I do not say “stop sending.”

I say “great, we found easy wins.”

We start to fix one by one. 
Small steps.
Low drama.

Fast forward a few weeks.

Leads land with the right owner.
Follow up is fast.
Reports make sense.

Now step 10 sounds actually fun.

Funny part?

The same team, same product, same market.

Only change is a cleaner system.

When your pipeline slows, where do you look first now, the send button or the engine under it?

I hate to say this. But the odds of:

- doubling outbound volume
- keeping the same GTM system
- expecting pipeline to finally be “predictable”

They’re extremely high.

And most teams only see the real problem when things start breaking.

Not because anyone made a bad decision. This is just how scaling works.

When you increase outbound volume, you expose things like:

- slow or manual lead routing
- no clear owner for each stage in the CRM
- response time is creeping from hours to days
- messy data and duplicates everywhere
- great leads sitting untouched because “no one saw it”

That’s a brutal environment for sales reps to properly perform.

The teams that scale outbound without chaos, rebuild the system behind it first:

- Fix routing and ownership before increasing volume
- Set response-time standards and monitor them (or automate managing the responses with our custom AI agents 😉)
- Clean the CRM and make hygiene a habit

Example from our clients:

Before we touch copy or add new sequences, we run what I call “Step 1–9”:

- proper data foundation (so there’s actually a system we can build something on top)
- clear owners for every stage
- leads auto-assigned by rules
- alerts for stuck deals and slow follow-up
- streamlined hand-off leads between teams
- simple, clean reporting that people trust

Only when this works, we turn up volume.

The fun part? Often small changes in routing, timing, and hygiene create more pipeline than sending thousands of extra emails.

Outbound isn’t the problem.

Most of the time, the system under it just isn’t ready yet.

column3: 100 dials a day and still no meetings?

100 dials a day and still no meetings?

Here's the thing nobody tells you:

Most of us were told cold calling is a numbers game

dial more → book more

But that only works if people actually pick up and don't hang up in 10 seconds.

So here’s a better way

→ do proper research before dialing (LinkedIn, recent news, mutual connections)

→ lead with a relevant observation, not your pitch

→ ask a question they'd want to answer

→ make it about their world, not your product

for example:

❌ "Hi, I'm calling about our sales automation tool..." 

✅ "Saw you just expanded to EMEA, curious how you're handling outbound there?"

The goal is to start a real conversation

cold call feels less interruptive this way

p.s. yes, this takes more time per call, but would you rather make 100 calls that go nowhere or 20 that actually lead somewhere?
